annotations.keyFindings: Peer support was associated with better engagement and hope in early psychosis, with no clear effect on readmission; peer roles varied widely.
annotations.limitations: Nine small studies, two randomised; uptake rarely reported.

annotations.keyFindings: A feasibility trial in two teams recruited 64 of a target of 80 in 12 months, retained 78 percent at six months, delivered a median of 1.8 peer contacts a week and had 70 percent questionnaire completion.
annotations.limitations: Two teams; completion lower in under-18s.

annotations.keyFindings: Forty percent of peer support workers left within a year, citing unclear roles and lack of lived-experience supervision.
annotations.limitations: Cross-sectional survey with interviews; community teams rather than early intervention.

annotations.keyFindings: Twenty-three percent disengaged within 12 months, most within six months, more often young men, daily cannabis users and people without stable housing.
annotations.limitations: Reasons recorded for a third; protective service features not assessed.

annotations.keyFindings: Young people wanted flexible contact and clear confidentiality rules; some families felt excluded by one-to-one contact.
Brief questionnaire completion fell from 74 to 58 percent by six months, lowest in under-18s; asking in person helped.

claims.text: Peer support in early psychosis was associated with better engagement and hope but no clear effect on readmission.
claims.passage: Peer support was associated with better engagement with services and higher scores on hope and recovery measures, but there was no clear effect on readmission or symptoms.
claims.interpretation: Engagement is the plausible target; readmission is not a feasibility outcome.

claims.text: A randomised feasibility trial of peer support in two early intervention teams recruited 64 of a target of 80 participants in 12 months and retained 78 percent at six months.
claims.passage: We recruited 64 participants, and 78 percent provided six-month outcome data.
claims.interpretation: Benchmarks for the progression criteria of this study.

claims.text: Forty percent of peer support workers in community teams left within a year, often citing unclear roles.
claims.passage: Forty percent of those surveyed had left their post within a year, most often citing unclear roles
claims.interpretation: Role clarity and lived-experience supervision must be part of the intervention and measured.

claims.text: About a quarter of young people disengaged from early intervention services within 12 months, mostly in the first six months.
claims.interpretation: Engagement over the first six months is the outcome a later trial would target.

synthesis: Six retrieved records, appraised at abstract level after the first reply arrived as prose and was not applied. Peer support in early psychosis is associated with better engagement and hope but not with fewer readmissions. A randomised feasibility trial in two teams recruited most of its target and retained most participants, giving benchmarks for progression criteria. Peer workers leave often when roles are unclear, a quarter of young people disengage within a year, and questionnaire completion falls among under-18s unless someone asks in person.
gradeRationale: One moderate-quality feasibility trial and otherwise small observational and qualitative studies; consistent in direction for engagement but imprecise and from few services.
summary: Six retrieved records appraised; four source-derived claims; overall certainty low.
